title: Scaling & Load Balancing Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on scaling a service: vertical vs horizontal, stateless design, load balancers (L4 vs L7), balancing algorithms, health checks, latency vs throughput and back-of-envelope estimation.

chapters.title: Scaling Mental Model
points: Vertical scaling (scale up): bigger machine (more CPU/RAM); simple, no code change, but hard ceiling, downtime on resize, single point of failure
Horizontal scaling (scale out): more machines behind a load balancer; near-linear capacity, fault tolerant, but needs stateless design and adds coordination complexity
Comparison row: vertical = limited + simple + SPOF; horizontal = elastic + resilient + complex (data consistency, networking)
Example: a 4-vCPU API at 90% CPU: resize to 16 vCPU (vertical) or add 3 identical 4-vCPU instances behind an LB (horizontal)
Mistake: scaling the app tier horizontally while the single database stays the bottleneck; the DB needs replicas, caching or sharding

chapters.title: Stateless Services
points: Stateless service: any request can be served by any instance because no per-user state lives in instance memory or local disk
Move state out: sessions to Redis/shared store, files to object storage (S3), data to the database; or put state in a signed token (JWT)
Stateless vs stateful: stateless instances are interchangeable, so they can be killed, replaced and autoscaled freely; stateful ones need sticky routing or replication
Example: login session stored in Redis keyed by session ID cookie, so request 2 can hit a different server than request 1 and still be logged in
Mistake: in-memory session or local-disk uploads behind an LB gives random logouts and missing files; the fix is a shared store, not sticky sessions as a crutch

chapters.title: Load Balancers: L4 vs L7
points: Load balancer: single entry point (VIP/DNS name) that spreads incoming traffic across healthy backend instances and hides their addresses
L4 (transport): routes on IP + TCP/UDP port, does not read payload; very fast, low overhead, protocol agnostic (e.g. AWS NLB)
L7 (application): reads HTTP (host, path, headers, cookies); enables path/host routing, TLS termination, rewrites, sticky cookies (e.g. AWS ALB, Nginx, HAProxy)
Comparison row: L4 = speed, any TCP/UDP, no content awareness; L7 = smarter routing, more CPU per request, can inspect and modify traffic
Mistake: the LB itself becomes a single point of failure; run it redundantly (multi-AZ, active-passive or DNS/anycast across several)

chapters.title: Balancing Algorithms and Health Checks
points: Round robin: rotate through servers in order; simple, assumes equal servers and similar request cost. Weighted round robin: bigger servers get proportionally more requests
Least connections: send to the server with fewest active connections; best when request durations vary widely (long-lived or uneven requests)
IP hash / consistent hashing: same client or key maps to the same server; gives affinity and cache locality, and consistent hashing limits remapping when servers join or leave
Health checks: LB probes each backend (TCP connect or HTTP GET /health expecting 200) every N seconds; after a failure threshold the instance is removed, after a success threshold it is re-added

Mistake: a shallow /health that returns 200 while the DB is down, or a deep check that hits the DB and takes every instance out at once; also no connection draining on removal drops in-flight requests

chapters.title: Latency, Throughput and Estimation
points: Latency = time for one request (ms, report p50/p95/p99, not just average); throughput = requests handled per second (QPS/RPS) or bytes per second
Relation: concurrency = throughput x latency (Little's law); 200 RPS at 50 ms latency means about 10 requests in flight
Throughput can rise by adding instances, while latency per request does not drop; tail latency (p99) grows as utilization nears 100%, so keep utilization around 60-70% (30-40% headroom)
Estimation recipe: DAU x actions/user/day / 86,400 = average QPS; peak is roughly 2-3x average; storage = writes/day x size x retention; bandwidth = QPS x payload size
Example: 10M DAU x 10 requests / 86,400 is about 1,150 QPS average, about 3,000 QPS peak; at 500 QPS per instance that is 6 instances plus a spare for N+1 redundancy
Mistake: sizing for average load instead of peak, ignoring p99, and forgetting that one day is about 100,000 seconds (a handy rounding for quick math)

chapters.title: Scaling Cheat Sheet
points: Vertical = bigger box (simple, capped, SPOF); horizontal = more boxes (elastic, needs stateless)
Stateless checklist: sessions in Redis, files in object storage, config from environment, no local state
L4 = IP/port, fast, any protocol; L7 = HTTP-aware, path/host routing, TLS termination
Algorithm picks: round robin (uniform), weighted (mixed sizes), least connections (uneven requests), hash (affinity)
Quick math: 1 day is about 86,400 s, peak is about 2-3x average, concurrency = RPS x latency, plan 60-70% utilization plus N+1 spare
